label: <DEL> delimiter step in longer sequences (L >= 6)
explanation: Fires only at the delimiter step (input <DEL>, t == L, which outputs original token 0); never in the original or copy phases. Within delimiter steps, firing rate and magnitude grow with sequence length: rate ~2% at L=3-4, ~4% at L=5, ~10-20% of all steps at t=6-9 (nearly every delimiter for L>=8), and the longest sequences (L=8,9) carry ~70% of activation mass. Weak activations come from short-sequence delimiters (L<=5), which the predicate misses. No dependence on token identity (out_tok, prev_tok, first_tok lifts are flat ~1-1.5x beyond the length effect) or digit count. phase==1 alone gives recall 1.0 but precision 0.65; adding L>=6 gives dev F1 0.89, mass recall 0.97.

issues: Minor: the misses aren't only short sequences. About 39% of L=6 delimiter steps are inactive, which is the largest false-positive class (L=6 precision 0.61). L=7 is about 97% active. L>=6 is a cutoff placed on what is really a gradual rise in firing rate with length. No token rule tested here explains the L=6 / L=5 boundary cases: n_digits, prev_tok matching orig(L-2) and out_count are all flat at about 0.60-0.62 precision.

Minor: 'token identity barely matters' slightly understates one effect. At L=6, a digit as the last original token (prev_tok) lowers the firing rate to 0.46, against 0.64 when it is a letter. Building that into the predicate does not improve test F1 (0.889 vs 0.890).

Every factual claim checks out. All activity is in phase 1, with none in the original or copy phases. L>=6 gives dev P 0.878 / R 0.902 / F1 0.890 / mass recall 0.969. Test F1 is 0.890. L>=7 alone gives F1 0.84, so L>=6 is the better cutoff.
